WHY THIS DOES NOT WEAKEN THE BEAD, and I want to be careful here because it would be easy to read it as deflation. Your central claim is that NO CONVENTION EXISTS, and the evidence is that adjacent methods disagree. That is a claim about how the code was WRITTEN, and it is unaffected by whether either method is called - two adjacent methods choosing opposite conventions proves nobody was applying one, whether or not anything consumes them. The SoftCompatibility pair is still your cleanest proof precisely because both methods are higher-is-better and adjacent.

What the partition changes is WHERE THE WORK GOES. Three sites feed inference and they are all in cost.scala; two feed only tests; one feeds only a report. A sweep that fixes fifteen sites uniformly spends most of its effort where nothing reads the answer, and - more to the point - it changes published numbers at three sites and cosmetics at the rest, which is a very different review.

NOTE THE OVERLAP YOU SHOULD KNOW ABOUT: all three inference sites are in cost.scala, and two of them (dSens, and the wire.scala bar that makes Semantic unrecordable) are already bd-01M16M5ETH0QHFZ62KXZJ54PN9 and bd-01M16S2Y6YS82TE6WBWQPKNZR3, both open and both awaiting the chief's ruling because they move published alignments. So the inference third of this sweep is blocked on the same ruling, and I should not start it independently.

NEXT unless redirected: partition the remaining nine sites the same way, then propose the policy on the completed table rather than on the six. I have touched none of them.
